Title: Anterior mediastinal nodular lesion segmentation from chest computed tomography imaging using UNet based neural network with attention mechanisms
Abstract: Automated detection of anterior mediastinal nodular lesions (AMLs) has significance for clinical usage as it is challenging for radiologists to accurately identify AMLs from chest computed tomography (CT) imaging due to various factors, including poor resolution, variations in intensity and the similarity of the AMLs to other tissues. To assist radiologists in AML detection from chest CT imaging, a UNet-based computer-aided detection (CADe) system is proposed to segment AMLs from slice images of the chest CT scans. The proposed network adopts a modified UNet architecture. To guide the proposed network to selectively focus on AMLs and potentially disregard others in the image, different attention mechanisms are utilized in the proposed network, including the self-attention mechanism and the convolutional block attention module (CBAM). The proposed network was trained and evaluated on 180 chest CT scans which consist of 180 AMLs. 90 AMLs were identified as thymic cysts, and 90 AMLs were diagnosed as thymoma. The proposed network achieved an average dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 93.23 with 5-fold cross-validation, for which the mean Intersection over Union (IoU), sensitivity and specificity were 90.29, 93.98 and 95.68 respectively. Our method demonstrated an improved segmentation performance over state-of-the-art segmentation networks, including UNet, ResUNet, TransUNet and UNet++. The proposed network employing attention mechanisms exhibited a promising result for segmenting AMLs from chest CT imaging and could be used to automate the AML detection process for achieving improved diagnostic reliability.

gold.abstract: To automatically detect Anterior Mediastinum Lesions (AMLs) in the Anterior Mediastinum (AM), the primary requirement will be an automatic segmentation model specifically designed for the AM. The prevalence of AML is extremely low, making it challenging to conduct screening research similar to lung cancer screening. Retrospectively reviewing chest CT scans over a specific period to investigate the prevalence of AML requires substantial time. Therefore, developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model to find location of AM helps radiologist to enhance their ability to manage workloads and improve diagnostic accuracy for AMLs. In this paper, we introduce a U-shaped structure network to segment AM. Two attention mechanisms were used for maintaining long-range dependencies and localization. In order to have the potential of Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and a lightweight network, we designed a parallel MHSA named Wide-MHSA (W-MHSA). Maintaining long-range dependencies is crucial for segmentation when we upsample feature maps. Therefore, we designed a Dilated Depth-Wise Parallel Path connection (DDWPP) for this purpose. In order to design a lightweight architecture, we introduced an expanding convolution block and combine it with the proposed W-MHSA for feature extraction in the encoder part of the proposed U-shaped network. The proposed network was trained on 2775 AM cases, which obtained an average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 87.83%, mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 79.16%, and Sensitivity of 89.60%. Our proposed architecture exhibited superior segmentation performance compared to the most advanced segmentation networks, such as Trans Unet, Attention Unet, Res Unet, and Res Unet++.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-c (Researcher B): Provides LCS eligibility variables—age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, YSQ, comorbidity-adjusted life expectancy—and emphasizes shared decision-making plus smoking cessation integration. I adopt these as static risk-stratification inputs.
- My prior proposal’s second contribution (Paper-d, design-science/operations): Provides a queuing or appointment-scheduling framework with capacity constraints and no-show prediction. I qualify this by requiring that Paper-d’s no-show model uses demographic/behavioral covariates compatible with LCS variables (age, smoking status, comorbidity), not generic clinic volume.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
The causal link is operational: Paper-c’s YSQ and comorbidity variables become inputs to Paper-d’s appointment-scheduling algorithm. Specifically, patients with high YSQ (>15) and low comorbidity burden are predicted to have lower no-show probability and longer safe screening intervals, so Paper-d’s scheduler assigns them lower-priority slots (e.g., off-peak times) while reserving high-priority slots for recent quitters (YSQ ≤5) with elevated comorbidity, who show higher adherence sensitivity to scheduling convenience. This is not keyword overlap; it uses Paper-d’s capacity model to act on Paper-c’s risk gradient.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Data: Retrospective cohort from a health system with LDCT scheduling records linked to smoking history (age, pack-years, YSQ, Charlson comorbidity index).
- Measurement: Compute each patient’s Paper-c risk tier; extract Paper-d no-show predictions from scheduling system logs (lead time, slot time, prior no-shows).
- Manipulation (simulation): Run Paper-d’s scheduler under two policies—(a) uniform slot assignment, (b) risk-weighted assignment using Paper-c variables.
- Validation: Compare no-show rates, time-to-next-screen adherence, and simulated false-positive/late-stage tradeoff over 3 years. Control for clinic capacity and seasonality already in Paper-d.
- Analysis: Difference-in-differences with inverse probability weighting for comorbidity; sensitivity test dropping YSQ to confirm it adds predictive value beyond pack-years alone.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We integrate ACS lung cancer screening risk variables with an appointment-scheduling model to test whether assigning screening slots by YSQ and comorbidity reduces no-shows and improves adherence without delaying high-risk patients. Using a retrospective cohort and scheduler simulation, we predict that risk-weighted slot assignment lowers no-show rates among recent quitters with comorbidities while maintaining guideline-concordant intervals for lower-risk patients. This would show that operational scheduling can be a behavioral adherence intervention, not just a capacity tool—beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: Use LCS risk variables (YSQ, comorbidity) as inputs to a capacity-constrained appointment scheduler to reduce no-shows and improve screening adherence through risk-weighted slot assignment.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-c (Researcher B): ACS 2023 LCS guidelines—annual LDCT for ages 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, YSQ, comorbidity-adjusted life expectancy, shared decision-making. I adopt the screening population and YSQ/comorbidity variables as the deployment context and risk-modifying covariates.
- Paper A (Researcher A): UNet with self-attention and CBAM for AML segmentation, DSC 93.23 on 180 scans (90 cysts, 90 thymomas). I adopt the segmentation model and attention maps as validated lesion delineation and interpretable feature generators. I qualify the thymic cyst/thymoma binary as insufficient for LCS incidental findings; I extend it to a triage task (no follow-up vs. short-interval vs. immediate).

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
The operational link is workflow-embedded: Paper A’s segmentation runs on every LDCT already acquired under Paper-c criteria. Attention-weighted features from the UNet become inputs to a triage classifier whose output is interpreted through Paper-c’s comorbidity-adjusted life expectancy. Specifically, a suspicious AML in a patient with high comorbidity and short life expectancy would be flagged for shared decision-making rather than automatic biopsy, while the same lesion in a low-comorbidity patient triggers immediate referral. This uses Paper-c’s life-expectancy logic to modulate Paper A’s output, not just co-occurrence.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Data: Retrospective LDCTs from an LCS registry meeting Paper-c criteria (N≈2,000 scans with incidental AMLs; pathology or 2-year stability as ground truth).
- Measurement: Apply Paper A’s UNet to delineate AMLs. Extract attention-weighted shape/texture features. Compute Paper-c variables (age, YSQ, Charlson comorbidity, life expectancy).
- Triage model: Three-class classifier (benign/no follow-up, indeterminate/short-interval, suspicious/immediate) using attention features plus Paper-c covariates.
- Validation: External LCS site; DSC for segmentation; AUC and decision-curve analysis for triage; compare against standard radiomics and against Paper A’s binary model. Report net reduction in unnecessary follow-up at fixed sensitivity for thymoma.
- Analysis: Stratify by life expectancy to test whether Paper-c modulation changes triage decisions without missing malignancies.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We integrate attention-based AML segmentation from chest CT into ACS lung cancer screening workflows to triage incidental anterior mediastinal lesions. The UNet provides interpretable attention features; ACS comorbidity-adjusted life expectancy modulates triage thresholds via shared decision-making. Using a multi-site LCS cohort, we test whether this combined approach reduces unnecessary follow-up for benign cysts while maintaining thymoma detection, compared to segmentation alone or guidelines alone. This contributes a clinically embedded, risk-modulated triage pathway beyond either source paper.

FINAL IDEA: Embedding attention-based AML segmentation within ACS lung cancer screening workflows creates a comorbidity-modulated triage system that reduces unnecessary follow-up while preserving malignant lesion detection.
